what_its_for: Norethindrone is a progestin (a type of female hormone) used to prevent pregnancy. It is also called the 'mini-pill' because it does not contain estrogen. Some forms are also used to treat irregular periods or endometriosis (a painful condition where tissue from the uterus grows outside of it).
how_to_take: Take this pill by mouth with or without food. Take it at the SAME TIME every day — try not to be more than 3 hours late. Taking it at the same time each day is very important for it to work properly. You may want to set a daily alarm to help you remember. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water.
dosing: The usual dose is one tablet (0.35 mg) every day, with no break between pill packs. Unlike combination birth control pills, there are no 'off' days — you take a pill every single day of the month. Your doctor may prescribe a different dose if you are using it for other reasons such as treating endometriosis.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose or take it more than 3 hours late, take the missed pill as soon as you remember. Use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the next 48 hours (2 days). If you have unprotected sex during this time, talk to your doctor or pharmacist about emergency contraception. Do NOT take two pills at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store norethindrone at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist about drug take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking cigarettes while taking any hormonal birth control, as it can increase your risk of serious side effects. Do not take this medication if you think you might already be pregnant. Avoid taking herbal supplements like St. John's Wort, as they can make this pill less effective. Certain medications like seizure medicines (such as phenytoin or carbamazepine) and HIV medicines may also make norethindrone less effective — always tell your doctor and pharmacist about everything you take.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: sudden severe headache, vision changes or blurred vision, chest pain or shortness of breath, severe abdominal (stomach) pain, swelling or pain in your legs, yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), or a new lump in your breast. Also call your doctor if you have no period for 2 months in a row or if you think you might be pregnant. Contact your doctor if you have ongoing irregular bleeding, severe mood changes, or depression.
when_it_works: If you start norethindrone on the first day of your period, it should protect you from pregnancy right away. If you start it at any other time during your cycle, use a backup birth control method (such as condoms) for the first 48 hours. It is important to take it consistently every day at the same time for it to work best. For other uses like treating endometriosis or irregular periods, it may take several weeks before you notice improvement.
special_populations: Breastfeeding mothers: Norethindrone (the mini-pill) is generally considered safe to use while breastfeeding and is often preferred over pills that contain estrogen. Teens: This medication can be used by teenagers who need birth control. Older adults/Perimenopause: May be used, but talk to your doctor about whether it is right for you. People with certain health conditions such as liver disease, unexplained vaginal bleeding, or a history of breast cancer should NOT take this medication — talk to your doctor about your full medical history before starting.
